To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

leukocytes from tuberculin-sensitive donors transfer delayed type sensitivity to human recipients, but leukocytic extracts from ragweed-sensitive donors do not transfer immediate type sensitivity to human subjects.

leukocyte extracts obtained from tuberculin sensitive patients can transfer delayed hypersensitivity to tuberculin to human skin, but leukocytic extracts obtained from allergic patients do not transfer immediate type hypersensitivity to ragweed, penicillin or horse serum.

leukocyte extracts from tuberculin-sensitive patients can sensitize tuberculin-negative recipients to tuberculin, but extracts from patients sensitive either to ragweed pollen and penicillin or to ragweed and tuberculin cannot sensitize tubercinun-negative recipients to ragweed pollen.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of leukocytes from allergic patients.
the transfer of delayed type skin sensitivity to human recipients by means and materials derived from human donors.
the study of leukocytosis and its possible relationship to the development of delayed type hypersensitivity and the transfer of delayed and immediate type hypersensitivity in human beings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

leukocytic extracts contain an unknown substance that is capable of transferring delayed-type hypersensitivity but that they do not contain skin sensitizing antibody or precipitins or antibodies capable of causing anaphylactic reactions.

(a) leukocytic extracts from tuberculin-sensitive patients contain a substance which can transfer delayed type tuberculin sensitivity, but (b) leukocytic antibodies against ragweed pollen or horse serum are not demonstrable by passive transfer.
leukocytic extracts obtained from patients sensitive only to tuberculin contain an unknown substance capable of transferring delayed-type skin sensitivity to human recipients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
leukocytic antibodies are not involved in immediate-type allergic responses.
the leukocytes from the peripheral blood are not the source of skin-sensitization antibodies against ragweed pollen.
leukocytes are not the site of formation of antibodies against ragweed pollen or horse serum.
The main takeaway from our work is that
leukocytes are not a source of skin-sensitization antibody in allergic patients.
we were unable to demonstrate the presence of antibodies in leukocytes which could be detected on passive sensitization.
we have shown that leukocytes can transfer delayed type sensitivity to human recipients, but that they do not appear to contain skin-sensitized antibody against ragweed, penicillin or horse serum.
